title: Causal Inference
description: Potential outcomes, confounding and selection bias, adjustment and propensity scores, causal diagrams, and quasi-experimental designs.
overview: Does a training program raise wages, does a drug cure, did the new feature increase retention? These are questions about what would happen if we intervened, and they are not answered by prediction alone. A model can predict wages very well from whether someone attended the program, and still say nothing about what the program does, because the people who attend differ from those who do not. Causal inference is the study of when, and with what assumptions, an effect can be learned from data.

This chapter introduces the potential outcomes framework, shows why a naive comparison is biased, explains what randomization and adjustment each achieve, presents causal diagrams for deciding what to adjust for (and what not to), and describes designs that exploit natural experiments: difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity and instrumental variables.
objectives: Define potential outcomes and the average treatment effect, and decompose the naive difference into effect plus selection bias.
State the assumptions (exchangeability, positivity, consistency) under which an effect is identified.
Estimate an effect by stratification, regression adjustment and inverse probability weighting with propensity scores.
Use causal diagrams to identify confounders, mediators and colliders, and apply the backdoor criterion.
Compute difference-in-differences and instrumental variable estimates, and describe regression discontinuity.

sections.title: Potential outcomes and the fundamental problem
body: Suppose you take an aspirin and your headache goes away. Did the aspirin work? To know, you would need to see what would have happened if you had not taken it, but you cannot go back and live the same moment twice. Only one of the two possible outcomes is ever observed. Causal inference is the set of methods for answering such questions anyway, by finding or creating comparison groups that stand in for the missing outcome. Let T = 1 if a unit receives the treatment and T = 0 otherwise. Each unit has two **potential outcomes**: Y(1), what would happen under treatment, and Y(0), what would happen without it. The causal effect for the unit is Y(1) − Y(0). The **fundamental problem of causal inference** is that we observe only one of the two: the outcome under the treatment actually received. The other is a **counterfactual**, never seen.

We can still hope to learn averages. The **average treatment effect** (ATE) is E[Y(1) − Y(0)]. The obvious estimate is the difference in observed means between the treated and untreated, E[Y | T = 1] − E[Y | T = 0]. It equals the ATE only if the two groups would have had the same outcomes absent treatment. In general
the average effect on the treated plus a **selection bias** term: the difference in the untreated outcomes of the two groups.

example.title: Selection bias with four units
example.problem: Four units have these potential outcomes (never all observable): A: Y(0) = 3, Y(1) = 5; B: 5, 6; C: 7, 9; D: 9, 10. Units C and D, the healthier ones, take the treatment; A and B do not. What are the true ATE and the naive difference?
solution: Observed: A and B untreated (Y = 3, 5; mean 4). C and D treated (Y = 9, 10; mean 9.5). The naive difference is 9.5 − 4 = 5.5, more than three times the true effect.
The effect on the treated (C and D) is (2 + 1)/2 = 1.5, and the selection bias is E[Y(0) | treated] − E[Y(0) | untreated] = 8 − 4 = 4, so 1.5 + 4 = 5.5. The treated were better off anyway.

body.h: What is needed to identify an effect

list: **Exchangeability** (ignorability, no unmeasured confounding): given the measured covariates X, treatment is independent of the potential outcomes, so that the treated and untreated are comparable within each X-stratum. Randomization guarantees it. In observational data it is an assumption that cannot be tested.
**Positivity** (overlap): every kind of unit has a chance of both treatment and no treatment, 0 < P(T = 1 | X) < 1. Where no comparable untreated units exist, the data say nothing about the effect.

**Consistency and no interference** (SUTVA): the observed outcome under the treatment received equals the potential outcome, treatment is well defined, and one unit's treatment does not affect another's outcome.

body.note: Questions about effects need assumptions that the data alone cannot verify. A good causal analysis states them, argues for them with subject-matter knowledge and tests their sensitivity (how strong would an unmeasured confounder have to be to explain away the result?).

sections.title: Randomization, stratification and propensity scores
body: In a randomized experiment treatment is independent of the potential outcomes by design, so the selection bias is zero and the naive difference estimates the ATE (see Sampling and Experiments). With observational data we try to make the groups comparable by conditioning on the confounders X.
Compare treated and untreated units //within// strata of X, then average the stratum effects with the weights of a common population. This is exactly the resolution of Simpson's paradox.

example.title: Adjusting the kidney stone data
example.problem: In the kidney stone data (see the Data Science Process chapter) treatment A succeeded in 93.1% of 87 small-stone cases and 73.0% of 263 large-stone cases; B in 86.7% of 270 small and 68.8% of 80 large. Compute the success rates standardized to the combined population of 357 small and 343 large stones.
example.solution: A: (357 × 0.931 + 343 × 0.730)/700 = (332.4 + 250.4)/700 = 83.3%. B: (357 × 0.867 + 343 × 0.688)/700 = (309.4 + 235.8)/700 = 77.9%. Adjusted for stone size, A is better by 5.4 points, the reverse of the naive overall comparison (78% versus 83%), because the naive comparison mixed up different case mixes.

body: Fit a regression of the outcome on the treatment and the confounders: the treatment coefficient is the adjusted effect (see Regression for Inference). It requires the model to be correctly specified, and does not warn when treated and untreated units overlap too little (it extrapolates).

When there are many confounders, stratifying on all of them is impossible. Rosenbaum and Rubin (1983) showed it is enough to condition on one number, the **propensity score**: e(x) = P(T = 1 | X = x), the probability of treatment given the covariates. It is estimated by a classifier (logistic regression, gradient boosting). It is used in three ways:

list: **Matching**: pair each treated unit with an untreated unit of similar propensity.

**Inverse probability weighting** (IPW): weight each unit by the inverse of the probability of the treatment it received, 1/e(x) for treated and 1/(1 − e(x)) for untreated units. The weighted groups mimic a population in which treatment was randomized. The effect estimate is the difference of the weighted means.

example.title: Inverse probability weights
example.problem: In a stratum of patients, 80% receive the treatment (e = 0.8). What weights do treated and untreated patients get, and what does this do?
example.solution: Treated: 1/0.8 = 1.25. Untreated: 1/0.2 = 5. The few untreated patients in this stratum stand in for the many that would be untreated if the treatment had been given at random, so they count five times. Units with propensities near 0 or 1 get huge weights and make the estimate unstable (a symptom of poor overlap); weights are often trimmed. Check that after weighting the covariates are balanced between the groups, and plot the propensity distribution in both groups.

body.warn: All these methods adjust only for //measured// confounders. If an important cause of both treatment and outcome (motivation, genetics, severity recorded only in a doctor's notes) is missing, the estimate is biased however sophisticated the method. Doubly robust estimators and 'causal machine learning' (double machine learning, causal forests) combine outcome models and propensity models to reduce the dependence on correct modeling, but they do not remove the need for no unmeasured confounding.

check.q: In inverse probability weighting, a treated unit with propensity score 0.25 receives weight

sections.title: Causal diagrams: confounders, mediators and colliders
body: Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in summer, so they are correlated, but ice cream does not cause drowning. Hot weather causes both. A causal diagram draws this as arrows: weather → ice cream and weather → drowning. The diagram makes the reasoning visible and tells you what to account for: here you would compare days of similar temperature before concluding anything. A **causal diagram** is a directed acyclic graph in which an arrow X → Y says that X is a direct cause of Y (see d-separation in Graphical Models). It encodes the analyst's assumptions about the data-generating process, and tells us what to adjust for. Three basic patterns on the path between a treatment T and an outcome Y:

head: Pattern
Diagram
Example
Adjust for Z?
rows: exercise causes both vitamin use and health
Yes: it opens a non-causal 'backdoor' path
a drug lowers blood pressure, which lowers heart attacks
No for the total effect: it removes part of the effect
talent and looks both cause being a celebrity

body.key: Backdoor criterion: the effect of T on Y is identified by adjusting for a set of variables Z if Z blocks every non-causal path from T to Y that begins with an arrow into T, and contains no descendant of T. Adjusting for common causes is right; adjusting for mediators, colliders and other consequences of the treatment is wrong.

example.title: Collider bias (Berkson's paradox)
example.problem: Among hospital patients, two unrelated diseases appear negatively associated. Why?
example.solution: Hospitalization is caused by either disease (a collider: A → H ← B). Restricting the data to patients means conditioning on H. Among the hospitalized, a patient who does not have disease A must have a reason to be there, so is more likely to have B: the diseases look negatively correlated although they are independent in the population. Similarly, among admitted students, test scores and extracurricular achievement are negatively correlated if admission needs either. Selecting a sample on an outcome or on a consequence of the variables of interest can create associations out of nothing.

list: **'Control for everything' is a bad strategy.** Adding every available variable to a regression can include colliders and mediators and make the estimate worse. Draw the diagram first.

**Post-treatment variables** (measured after treatment) are rarely safe to adjust for. In an experiment, comparing groups defined by a post-treatment variable (the 'responders') breaks the randomization.
The diagram expresses assumptions from domain knowledge; the data can test some of its implications (conditional independencies) but not the arrows themselves.
**Mediation analysis** separates the direct effect of T on Y from the effect through the mediator Z, with additional assumptions.

check.q: Which variable should be adjusted for when estimating the total effect of T on Y?
check.a: A common cause of T and Y (a confounder)
wrong: A variable caused by both T and Y (a collider)
A variable on the causal path from T to Y (a mediator)
Any variable in the data set

sections.title: Natural experiments: difference-in-differences, discontinuities and instruments
body: When confounders cannot all be measured and an experiment is impossible, a **quasi-experimental** design may exploit a feature of how treatment was assigned that is as good as random for some purpose.

A policy is introduced in one region (treated) and not in another (control). Compare the change over time in the treated region with the change in the control region. The control's change estimates what would have happened to the treated region without the policy, so that fixed differences between the regions and common time trends cancel:

example.title: A difference-in-differences estimate
example.problem: Average employment (in thousands) in a state that raised its minimum wage: 10 before, 16 after. In a neighboring state without the change: 8 before, 11 after. Estimate the effect.
example.solution: Treated change: 16 − 10 = +6. Control change: 11 − 8 = +3. DiD = 6 − 3 = +3. The naive before–after comparison (+6) would attribute the common upward trend (+3) to the policy. The estimate rests on the **parallel trends** assumption: without the policy both states would have changed by the same amount. Check by comparing the trends in the periods before the policy.

body: When treatment is assigned by a threshold on a continuous score (a scholarship for a test score of at least 80, a drug for blood pressure above a cutoff), people just above and just below the cutoff are nearly identical, differing only by chance in which side they fall. The jump in the outcome at the cutoff estimates the effect for units near it. It needs that the score cannot be precisely manipulated, and gives a local estimate.

An **instrument** Z affects the treatment T, affects the outcome Y only through T (the exclusion restriction), and is unrelated to the unmeasured confounders. Examples: a random encouragement, a lottery (the draft lottery for military service), distance to a college. Because Z is as good as random, it creates variation in T that is free of confounding. With a binary instrument the **Wald estimator** is the effect of Z on Y divided by the effect of Z on T:

example.title: An instrumental variable estimate
example.problem: Half the people receive a random reminder (Z = 1) to take a training course. Average earnings are 2.0 higher in the reminded group, and course take-up is 40% higher (60% versus 20%). What is the effect of the course?
example.solution: The reminder changes take-up by 0.4 and earnings by 2.0, so each additional person who takes the course because of the reminder gains 2.0/0.4 = 5.0. This is the **local average treatment effect** for those whose behavior the instrument changes (compliers), not necessarily the effect for people who would take the course regardless. The estimate is only as credible as the exclusion restriction: the reminder must affect earnings only by way of the course. In regression form it is two-stage least squares.

list: Each design buys credibility with a specific, checkable-in-part assumption (parallel trends, no manipulation of the score, the exclusion restriction) and answers a narrower question.

**Heterogeneous effects**: the effect often varies across people. Estimate it by subgroups or with causal ML (causal forests, meta-learners). **Uplift modeling** targets those for whom the treatment helps most (send the offer to customers whose purchase probability rises because of it, not those who would buy anyway).

**Prediction is not intervention**: a model that predicts churn well says who will leave, not who can be retained by an offer. Decisions about actions need causal estimates, typically from experiments.

wrong: the two groups are identical before the intervention
the intervention has the same effect on everyone
outcomes are never affected by time

check.q: An instrument must affect the outcome
wrong: directly, bypassing the treatment
not at all, not even through the treatment
only for the control group

quiz.q: Four units have potential outcomes (Y(0), Y(1)) of (4, 7), (6, 7), (5, 9) and (8, 8). The average treatment effect is
quiz.why: The unit effects are 3, 1, 4 and 0, whose mean is 2.0 (equivalently 7.75 − 5.75). The value 7.75 is only the mean of Y(1).

quiz.q: Treated units have an observed mean outcome of 20 and untreated units 14. Without treatment the treated units would have averaged 17. The average effect on the treated is
quiz.why: The naive difference 6 equals the effect on the treated plus selection bias, and the bias is 17 − 14 = 3. So the effect is 6 − 3 = 3.

quiz.q: In a study of a new drug, no patient over 80 years old received it. For which assumption does this create a problem when estimating the effect in that age group?
wrong: Exchangeability
Consistency
Parallel trends
quiz.why: Positivity requires every kind of unit to have some chance of both treatment and no treatment. With no treated patients over 80 the data say nothing about the effect there.

quiz.q: Vaccinating one person lowers the infection risk of that person's neighbors. Which assumption does this break?
quiz.a: No interference between units (part of SUTVA)
wrong: Positivity of treatment assignment given the covariates
Exchangeability
The exclusion restriction
quiz.why: The no-interference assumption says that one unit's treatment does not affect another unit's outcome. Here the neighbors' outcomes depend on someone else's treatment.

quiz.q: Treatment A has success rates 80% in mild cases and 50% in severe cases. A standard population is 60% mild and 40% severe. The standardized success rate for A is
quiz.why: 0.6 × 0.80 + 0.4 × 0.50 = 0.68. The simple average of the strata (65%) ignores the case mix, and swapping the weights gives 62%.

quiz.q: A patient who did not receive the treatment has a propensity score of 0.9. In inverse probability weighting this patient gets weight
quiz.why: An untreated unit is weighted by 1/(1 − e) = 1/0.1 = 10. Using 1/e = 1.11 is the weight for treated units.

quiz.q: Which problem is NOT solved by matching, weighting or double machine learning on the measured covariates?
quiz.a: A common cause of treatment and outcome that was never measured
wrong: Different mixes of age and severity in the treated and untreated groups
A treatment decision that depends on measured covariates
Strong imbalance in a measured confounder
quiz.why: These methods adjust only for what is measured. Clever modeling cannot compensate for a missing confounder, though it can fix imbalance in recorded variables.

quiz.q: Among hired applicants, GPA and interview skill are negatively correlated, although they are unrelated among all applicants. Why?
quiz.a: Hiring depends on both, so looking only at hired applicants conditions on a collider
wrong: GPA and interview skill really are opposing traits
Interviewers are systematically biased against candidates who have high GPAs and strong credentials
A confounder causes both GPA and interview skill
quiz.why: If a low GPA is to be hired, the applicant needs strong interviews, and vice versa. Selecting on a common effect creates an association out of nothing (Berkson's paradox).

quiz.q: A drug lowers blood pressure, and lower blood pressure reduces heart attacks. To estimate the drug's total effect on heart attacks, adjusting for blood pressure would
quiz.a: remove the part of the effect that runs through blood pressure, underestimating the total effect
wrong: remove confounding and give the correct total effect
create a spurious association by conditioning on a collider
leave the estimate unchanged, because blood pressure is measured after the treatment and so cannot matter
quiz.why: Blood pressure is a mediator on the causal path. Holding it fixed blocks the very route by which the drug works.

quiz.q: W is a common cause of treatment T and outcome Y. M lies on the path T → M → Y. C is caused by both T and Y. To estimate the total effect of T on Y, adjust for
wrong: W and M
W and C
M and C
quiz.why: The backdoor criterion requires blocking non-causal paths from T to Y without including descendants of T. Mediator M and collider C are both descendants of T.

quiz.q: In a randomized trial an analyst compares the two arms only among "responders", defined by an improvement in an early measurement taken after treatment began. Why is this comparison unreliable?
quiz.a: Response is a post-treatment variable, so the responders in each arm are no longer comparable groups
wrong: Responders are too few to compute a mean
The control arm cannot have any responders
Randomization only protects comparisons of the first measurement taken, and not any later measurement of the outcome
quiz.why: Treatment can change who becomes a responder, so selecting on response breaks the randomization. Comparisons should use the groups as originally assigned.

quiz.q: Employment in a treated state goes from 30 to 34 and in a control state from 25 to 31. The difference-in-differences estimate of the policy effect is
quiz.why: The treated change is +4 and the control change is +6, so DiD = 4 − 6 = −2. The before–after change alone (4) ignores the trend in the control state.

quiz.q: Before a policy, the treated region's outcome was already growing faster than the control region's. What is the consequence for a difference-in-differences estimate?
quiz.a: Parallel trends is doubtful, so part of the faster growth would be credited to the policy
wrong: The estimate becomes exactly zero, because the pre-existing difference in trends cancels out the policy effect
The estimate is unbiased as long as the groups' starting levels differ
Only the control group's baseline level matters
quiz.why: DiD relies on both groups moving alike without the policy. If their pre-trends already differ, the extra growth would be wrongly credited to the policy.

quiz.q: Scholarships go to students scoring at least 80. In a regression discontinuity analysis, the estimated effect mainly applies to
wrong: all students in the sample
students scoring far above 80
only students who would have enrolled anyway
quiz.why: Only near the cutoff are the two sides comparable, differing just by chance in which side they fall. The estimate is therefore local, not an average over the whole range of scores.

quiz.q: A random reminder raises course take-up from 30% to 55% and raises average test scores by 3 points. The instrumental variable (Wald) estimate of the course effect is
wrong: 0.083 points
3 points
0.75 points
quiz.why: The effect of the instrument on the outcome (3) is divided by its effect on take-up (0.25), giving 12. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 0.75.

quiz.q: Distance to the nearest college is used as an instrument for years of schooling when estimating the effect on earnings. Which situation would violate the exclusion restriction?
quiz.a: Living near a college changes local job opportunities, which affect earnings directly
wrong: Living near a college makes people more likely to study longer
Distance to college is unrelated to unmeasured ability
Some people go to college regardless of distance
quiz.why: The instrument may affect earnings only through schooling. A direct path from distance to earnings breaks that condition, while the other options describe relevance, independence and the existence of non-compliers.

quiz.q: A churn model predicts very accurately who will leave. Why is it not enough on its own to decide who should get a retention offer?
quiz.a: It tells who is likely to leave, not whose behavior the offer would change
wrong: Accurate models cannot be used for decisions about individuals
Customers likely to leave never respond to offers
Retention offers always lower the churn probability for everyone
quiz.why: Prediction is not intervention. Some likely leavers cannot be retained, and some would stay anyway, so deciding who to target needs an estimate of the effect of the offer, as in uplift modeling.

summary: Potential outcomes Y(1), Y(0): only one is observed per unit. The ATE is E[Y(1) − Y(0)]. The naive difference equals the effect on the treated plus selection bias, which can be large and of either sign.
Effects are identified under exchangeability (no unmeasured confounding), positivity and consistency. Randomization guarantees exchangeability.

With observational data adjust for measured confounders by stratification, regression, matching or inverse probability weights 1/e(x), 1/(1 − e(x)) using the propensity score. Unmeasured confounding remains a threat; check balance and overlap.
Causal diagrams show what to adjust for: confounders yes (backdoor criterion), mediators and colliders no. Conditioning on a collider creates spurious associations (Berkson's paradox).

Natural experiments: difference-in-differences (parallel trends), regression discontinuity (jump at a threshold) and instrumental variables (Wald: effect of Z on Y divided by effect of Z on T). Prediction and causation are different tasks.

problems.q: A job-training program is voluntary. Participants earn $42,000 on average a year later, non-participants $35,000. List two reasons the $7,000 difference may not be the program's effect, and one design that would give a credible estimate.
problems.solution: Participants may be more motivated or skilled (selection bias: they would have earned more anyway), and those who enrolled may differ in age or education. A credible design: randomize who is offered a place (or randomly select from oversubscribed applicants), or use the randomized offer as an instrument.
problems.a: Selection on motivation and background; a randomized offer.

problems.q: Treated region: crime rate 50 before, 44 after a new policy. Control region: 40 before, 38 after. Compute the difference-in-differences estimate.
problems.solution: Treated change = −6, control change = −2, so DiD = −6 − (−2) = −4: the policy is estimated to have reduced the crime rate by 4 points, compared with the −6 of the naive before–after comparison.

problems.q: In a randomized encouragement design, those encouraged earn on average 1.2 more, and 30% more of them enroll in a program than among the not encouraged. Estimate the effect of the program on compliers.
Draw the diagram for: smoking → tar deposits → lung cancer, and a genotype that causes both smoking and cancer. Which variables must be adjusted for to estimate the total effect of smoking on cancer?
problems.solution: Smoking ← Genotype → Cancer is a backdoor path: adjust for the genotype if measured. Tar deposits are a mediator on the path smoking → tar → cancer: do not adjust for them if the total effect is wanted. (If the genotype is unmeasured, the effect is not identified by adjustment alone; a front-door argument through tar, or an instrument, could help.)
problems.a: Adjust for genotype (the confounder); do not adjust for tar (the mediator).

problems.q: Treatment is more likely for sicker patients, who also have worse outcomes. In a data set, treated patients have worse outcomes than the untreated. Does the treatment harm? What could you do?
problems.solution: Not necessarily: this is confounding by indication. Severity causes both treatment and poor outcomes. Compare patients of similar severity (stratify, regress on severity, weight by propensity scores based on severity), check overlap, and, if possible, use a randomized study or an instrument (such as hospital practice patterns).
problems.a: Not necessarily; adjust for severity or use randomization.
